title: This too trains
hookLine: how to bear a fever: this too is exercise (Discourses 3.10)
last: FOUND DOING THIS — ATTENDING TO NOTHING BUT MY OWN WILL.

lines: ANCIENT WRITERS SAY HE WAS LAME.
cards: The thermometer beeps, and the week's plans quietly fall apart. Meetings get canceled, the to-do list sits there, and on top of feeling awful it's easy to feel useless, as if life is on pause until you're well.
Epictetus knew something about bodies that don't cooperate. Ancient writers say he was lame. When he talks about illness, he isn't speaking from a healthy distance.

teach.b: Discourses book three, chapter ten: how we should bear illness. It starts like a packing list.
Keep your principles ready for each situation: at the table, the ones about eating; in the bath, the ones about bathing; in bed, the ones about lying in bed. And the ones about fever.

teach.h: A FEVER IS PART OF LIFE TOO.
teach.b: A fever, he says, is part of life too, like walking, sailing or traveling. It isn't a pause. It's a different kind of practice.
So what does bearing a fever well look like? He's specific.
Not blaming God or other people. Not being crushed by what's happening. Doing what needs to be done.
When the doctor comes in, not dreading what he'll say, and not giddy if he says you're doing well. The same things he asks on a healthy day, in a smaller room. This too is training, he says.
A sick day isn't a day off from becoming who you want to be. In some ways it's a clear day for it, because the usual props are gone. You can't prove anything by being busy.
You can only be patient, honest about how you feel, and kind to whoever brings the soup. This isn't a reason to ignore medicine or push through when your body needs rest.
The person lying there is still training, and still free.

how: Some Stoic practitioners who are ill treat recovery as part of their practice: following medical care, resting, and working on patience rather than blame.

o: sickness, which Epictetus says can be borne as practice
a weakness you should push through without rest
a fever that keeps you from all your training

games.q: this too trains: tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says illness puts your practice on pause
he says a fever is part of life, and bearing it well is training too.
ancient writers say Epictetus was lame
so he speaks about bodies from experience.
bearing a fever well means ignoring the doctor
it means not dreading or overreacting to the news, while doing what needs to be done.

games.q: you're stuck in bed with a fever and feel useless. what does Epictetus say?
o: wait it out; nothing counts until you're well.
this too is part of life, and bearing it well is practice.
games.why: he says a fever is part of life like walking or sailing, and bearing it without blame or despair is training.

practice: Sit or lie down, whichever is kinder to your body right now, and scan gently from head to feet, noticing any ache, tiredness or tightness without fighting it or dramatizing it. Say plainly: this is here.
Then ask how you'd like to carry it today: with patience, with honesty, or simply by resting well.

wordCard.voice: Nosos. Greek for sickness: Epictetus on illness, a fever is part of life, and bearing it well, without blame or despair, is practice like any other.

orig.note: Greek nosos: sickness, disease; Discourses 3.10 is on how to bear it.

carryVoice: Your line: resting well is the practice. A fever is part of life, and so is bearing it well. Day four hundred nineteen, done.

sources.ref: Origen, Against Celsus 7.53; Simplicius, Commentary on the Enchiridion
